paper_title: WeMM-Ecom: Advancing Multimodal Content Understanding for WeChat E-Commerce

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: We present WeMM-Ecom, a family of multimodal large language models that deliver frontier e-commerce capabilities while achieving state-of-the-art general-purpose performance at their respective scales. The family spans five sizes, from a 0.8B dense model to a 35B mixture-of-experts model with 3B active parameters. Our training pipeline begins with two-stage continued pre-training that progressively raises the proportion of e-commerce data within a diverse multimodal data mixture, followed by hybrid-thinking post-training that combines on-policy distillation and reinforcement learning to support both non-thinking and thinking modes. For evaluation, we construct a comprehensive suite of 28 e-commerce benchmarks (23 in-house and five open-source) covering eight business scenarios and complement it with 64 public general-purpose benchmarks. On the e-commerce suite, WeMM-Ecom-35B-A3B surpasses substantially larger open-source flagship models, including Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, HY4, and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. On the general-purpose suite, every WeMM-Ecom model surpasses its similarly sized Qwen3.5 counterpart, with the lightweight variants (e.g., WeMM-Ecom-2B) showing clear advantages over leading lightweight models such as Qwen3.5-2B, MiniCPM-V-4.7-1B, and LFM3-VL-2B. Beyond benchmarks, WeMM-Ecom now powers hundreds of production use cases in WeChat, including catalog management, multimodal product search, and livestream commerce, serving billion-scale requests per day. We publicly release all model weights and detail our data curation, training recipe, and benchmark construction to facilitate future work on domain-specialized multimodal models. We have released the model weights and code to facilitate future research at https://github.com/Tencent/WeMM-Ecom.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have become capable general-purpose models for understanding images, documents, and video [24, 25, 27, 69, 78, 79, 86]. In specialized domains, however, general capability alone falls short, as models must apply fine-grained domain knowledge to what they see, whether identifying clinical finding in medical scan [72] or extracting the correct figure from financial chart [50]. E-commerce is an especially demanding domain for MLLMs. product can be presented through dozens of product views, long-form detail images, and livestream frames, alongside titles and structured attribute tables. Critical evidence, such as selling points, nutrition facts, dimension annotations, and certification marks, often appears only inside images. Models must further link this visual text to the specific SKU variant in question and draw on catalog knowledge that is never explicitly stated. As e-commerce models move from text records [39, 52, 61] to multimodal understanding [7, 91], two core challenges stand out: (1) models must accurately perceive dense, interleaved visual evidence and produce outputs that satisfy strict entity-level and business-rule constraints; and (2) domain specialization must not erode general visual perception and reasoning, especially for lightweight models deployed under tight latency and memory budgets [42, 99]. To address these challenges, we present WeMM-Ecom, family of multimodal foundation models spanning four dense sizes (0.8B, 2B, 4B, and 9B) and 35B mixture-of-experts (MoE) model with 3B active parameters (35B-A3B), initialized from Qwen3.5 [69]. We curate over 40 e-commerce tasks from product images, livestream frames, and business workflows. Because these tasks directly exercise visual grounding, OCR, and multi-image reasoning, they also strengthen general perception rather than competing with it. We pair them with broad general supervision in two-stage continued pre-training (CPT) curriculum with an increased e-commerce share in the second stage (Figure 3). Post-training then applies hybrid-thinking on-policy distillation (OPD), single parameter-space merge with the post-trained Qwen3.5 weights that recovers general instruction-following and reasoning abilities, and group relative policy optimization (GRPO), enabling each model to support both thinking and non-thinking modes. We evaluate WeMM-Ecom on comprehensive 28-benchmark e-commerce suite across eight scenarios (207,117 instances) and 64 general benchmarks. Across all five sizes and both modes, WeMM-Ecom consistently outperforms size-matched Qwen3.5 on e-commerce. WeMM-Ecom-35B-A3B ranks first among evaluated flagships (Figure 1), surpassing Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, HY4, and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017. In non-thinking mode, our 0.8B and 2B models each beat larger Qwen3.5 model on e-commerce while showing clear advantages on general-purpose capabilities. WeMM-Ecom-2B also surpasses MiniCPM-V-4.7-1B [99] and LFM3-VL-2B [42] on both e-commerce and general suites in both thinking and non-thinking modes. Our main contributions are as follows: 1. We open-source WeMM-Ecom, family of five multimodal models ranging from 0.8B dense model to 35B-A3B MoE model, each supporting both thinking and non-thinking modes. WeMM-Ecom delivers leading e-commerce performance at every scale while matching or surpassing its Qwen3.5 counterpart on general benchmarks, and has been validated at scale in production. 2. We present detailed training and data recipe for WeMM-Ecom. We describe how more than 40 e-commerce tasks are constructed from product images, livestream frames, and business records; how they are mixed with general data and scheduled across two CPT stages; and how hybrid-thinking OPD, one-time parameter-space merge, and GRPO are combined to produce the final models. 3. We introduce the key design principles of our e-commerce evaluation framework. We show how real-world business workflows are translated into eight evaluation scenarios with explicit inputs, decision targets, and scoring rules, resulting in suite of 23 in-house and five public benchmarks with 207,117 instances.

sections.content: We initialize each WeMM-Ecom model from the corresponding Qwen3.5 Base checkpoint [69] and perform full-parameter optimization across all training stages using the WeChat-YATT framework [90]. The resulting checkpoints support thinking and non-thinking modes and are evaluated on e-commerce and general benchmarks. broad multimodal capabilities. Subsequently, post-training combines OPD for token-level teacher guidance, single parameter-space merge with the post-trained Qwen3.5 weights, and reinforcement learning (RL) driven by task-specific verifiable rewards. All five model scales support thinking and non-thinking modes in unified chat interface. Figure 2 summarizes the training and evaluation pipeline.

sections.title: 2.1.1 E-Commerce Data
sections.content: General multimodal corpora teach model to recognize bag of coffee beans; e-commerce applications must also determine which variant it isthe 250 or the 500 SKU, single bag or two-packwhether its listing complies with platform rules, and how to present it to shoppers. We therefore design e-commerce supervision around three properties that general corpora rarely provide: variant-level granularity, traceable evidence, and rule-conditioned outputs. The five domains in Table 1 instantiate these properties in different combinations. Variant-level granularity. Product Perception & Understanding trains the model to resolve products at the level of categories, attributes, and SKUs. Category prediction pairs product images with taxonomy labels and reasoning traces, and attribute tasks extract visible text, properties, and regions from gallery images, detail strips, and livestream frames. SKU attribute examples specify variant and an attribute, supply the relevant views and fields, and use the recorded value as the target; net-weight question, for instance, must distinguish the 250 SKU from the 500 SKU. Product Retrieval applies the same granularity to matching. Each example pairs two listings, SKU records, or product regions with their available images and specifications, and defines equivalence at the requested level: single 500 bag and two-pack of 250 bags may depict the same product and contain the same total quantity, yet their pack configurations make them distinct SKUs. Region-level and cross-image examples extend matching to comparisons between specified visual entities. Traceable evidence. We tie targets to the evidence that supports them so that outputs can be checked against the source listing. SKU attribute examples retain the index of the source image that contains the recorded value. Bounding-box annotations localize products, brand logos, certification marks, specification tables, and dimension annotations, and explicitly mark targets that are absent from the image. In General E-Commerce Knowledge & QA, listing images, descriptions, visible text, and structured fields are paired with questions on product knowledge, commerce OCR, and reasoning, with reference answers supported by the supplied sources. Product descriptions, entity annotations, and articles further connect product appearance with names, brands, uses, and business knowledge. Rule-conditioned outputs. Many e-commerce decisions are defined by platform rules rather than by visual content alone. Product Information Audit pairs listing titles, gallery images, and attribute fields with platform governance rules and annotated compliance decisions. Its tasks include identifying restricted goods, detecting imagetitle or category inconsistencies, reviewing product-image quality, and screening content for policy violations; each target specifies the applicable rule and the decision, together with visual or textual evidence for tasks that require an explanation. The same domain also covers quality review of short product titles, where the target is set of pass/fail judgments rather than rewritten title. E-Commerce Content Generation applies rules to generation rather than judgment: short-title examples map structured product specifications to concise, formatted titles that follow platform style guidelines.

sections.title: 2.1.2 General-Purpose Data
sections.content: The seven general domains preserve the perception, language, knowledge, and reasoning capabilities that e-commerce tasks build on and that the model needs beyond them. They draw on curated sources and task mixtures, including all 162 nonempty sources in OpenBee [107]. We summarize the main sources below and describe shared construction procedures in Section 2.1.3. Perception and reading. Multimodal Understanding pairs images with Chinese or English captions and adds video data for event understanding and temporally grounded tasks, including sports event narration and general video question answering. OCR, Documents, and Charts pairs natural images, documents, charts, and tables with transcriptions, reading questions, or structured extraction targets, covering both the recognition of visible text and its use in document and chart understanding; sources include ChartNet [36], multilingual OCR collections, web articles, and table annotations. Grounding and Detection converts object and region annotations from Objects365 [73], SA-1B [35], and LocateAnything [85] into localization and detection targets conditioned on object names or referring descriptions, while GUI examples associate interface instructions with the locations of the corresponding elements. 5 Reasoning and knowledge. Visual Instruction & Reasoning combines single-image QA, multi-image comparison, visual quality assessment, and instruction-driven tasks. Each example pairs the available views with question or constrained instruction and reference answer, comparison judgment, or decision; multiimage questions require integrating evidence across views, and edit-instruction examples ask the model to infer, from source image and its edited version, the instruction that produced the change. Risk assessment and content moderation tasks apply written platform policies to general content such as short videos; unlike Product Information Audit, they do not review product listings. Multimodal STEM pairs diagramand video-based problems in mathematics, science, and technical reasoning with worked solutions, including material from Innovator-VL [89], and adds chart and document problems from educational corpora across biology, chemistry, mathematics, and K-12 science. Multimodal World Knowledge associates images with encyclopedic and entity-specific descriptions from online wikis and entity recaption sources, and pairs visual evidence with specialized questions whose answers draw on knowledge beyond the visible appearance. Text-only data. Pure Text retains general records without visual inputs as language and instruction supervision. Mathematical and scientific reasoning dominate this mixture, drawing on Nemotron-Math [17] and Chinese STEM sources, while instruction-following and multilingual dialogues, Wikipedia text, readingcomprehension QA, and curated web text supply general language, factual knowledge, and instruction-following supervision.

sections.title: 2.1.3 Data Construction and Quality Control
sections.content: Several construction and filtering procedures are shared across domains. Spatial targets and absent objects. Conversion of box annotations in both pools makes coordinate normalization explicit, preserves the source category schemas, and keeps each target linked to its annotated visual entity. Both pools also encode absence explicitly: e-commerce annotations mark targets missing from the image, and general grounding data includes rejection examples whose queries name objects absent from the image, teaching the model to decline rather than hallucinate box. Recaptioning. We cluster images with WeMM-Embedding [109], sample across clusters for recaptioning, and deduplicate the resulting captions. For text-rich images, PaddleOCR [10] transcriptions provide textual cues for caption generation. Synthesized reasoning. For synthesized STEM solutions, Qwen3.5-122B-A10B generates the reasoning and Qwen3.5-35B-A3B checks answer agreement; malformed or truncated solutions are discarded. Web article mining. Two classifiers identify product-recommendation articles and select comparative reviews or detailed accounts of product use. Qwen3.5-122B-A10B then filters promotional or irrelevant material and extracts product and brand facts, which we deduplicate with MinHash. Source balancing. When aggregating multi-source collections, we assign token budget to each source group and, where group exceeds its budget, downsample its constituent sources in proportion to their token counts, so that every source remains represented.

sections.title: 2.1.4 CPT Recipe
sections.content: Progressive data mixture. We adopt two-stage curriculum that increases domain specialization while maintaining broad general supervision (Figure 3). Stage 1 establishes multimodal and product representations with 45.8% e-commerce share, and Stage 2 raises the share to 61.1%. Within the e-commerce pool (percentages are shares within each pool), supervision shifts from basic perception toward compliance auditing and knowledge-intensive QA: Product Information Audit rises from 6.4% to 18.0%, General E-Commerce Knowledge & QA from 24.7% to 31.4%, and Product Perception & Understanding falls from 37.5% to 23.6%. Within the general pool, supervision shifts from captioning and text-only data toward dense text reading 6 and visually grounded reasoning: OCR, Documents, and Charts rises from 13.7% to 23.8% and Multimodal STEM from 2.9% to 19.0%, while Multimodal Understanding falls from 26.4% to 8.1% and Pure Text from 26.7% to 19.2%. Throughout CPT, we track per-domain validation losses to guide mixture adjustments. Training schedule and objective. All model sizes follow the same two-stage CPT schedule: Stage 1 trains on 370.3B tokens at 16K sequence length, and Stage 2 extends the context window to 32K for 76.7B tokens. sections.title: 2.2 Post-Training
sections.content: Following CPT, our post-training pipeline combines OPD, parameter-space model merging, and GRPO-based reinforcement learning. Both post-training stages optimize single set of weights to support both thinking and non-thinking modes [99].

sections.title: 2.2.1 Post-Training Data
sections.content: The post-training corpus spans general reasoning, visual perception, and instruction following alongside core e-commerce workflows such as variant matching and product detection. All model sizes share curated pool of 499,998 OPD promptsincluding specialist data for open-vocabulary detection, complex counting, and long-document QAand 30,976 prompts for RL. We select OPD prompts via offline teacherstudent comparisons, retaining instances where the teacher achieves higher mean quality score than the student. For RL, we sample multiple rollouts from the corresponding post-OPD merged checkpoint and retain prompts with positive reward variance while filtering out already saturated instances (Appendix A.1).

sections.title: 2.2.2 Hybrid Thinking
sections.content: To support both deliberative chain-of-thought reasoning (thinking mode) and low-latency direct responses (non-thinking mode) within single checkpoint, both OPD and RL assign training prompts to thinking and non-thinking modes at 4:1 ratio (Appendix A.1). Because per-response loss averaging assigns lower per-token weight to final answer tokens in longer reasoning traces, allocating higher proportion of prompts to thinking mode balances supervision across both paradigms. During RL, all rollouts within prompt group share the same operating mode.

sections.title: 3 E-Commerce Evaluation Framework
sections.content: Evaluating multimodal models for real-world commerce requires testing whether they can interpret complex product listings, align variants across views, enforce platform governance rules, and localize advertised items in livestream frames. We construct comprehensive evaluation suite of 28 benchmarkscomprising 23 in-house benchmarks and five public benchmarks, totaling 207,117 evaluation instancesorganized into the eight core 8 scenarios illustrated in Figure 4. Because the in-house benchmarks derive from proprietary business data, we detail their task definitions, input modalities, and scoring metrics in Appendix B. To prevent data contamination between training and business evaluation splits, we enforce strict deduplication across splits using product identifiers, cryptographic hashes for exact image duplicates, perceptual hashes for near duplicates, and visual embedding similarity. Figure 4 Overview of the eight e-commerce evaluation scenarios. Seven in-house scenarios are organized around an illustrative product listing into evidence extraction, product interpretation, and decision making, with representative prompts and target outputs (green), complemented by five public benchmarks in E-commerce (Open). Numbers in gray denote instance counts. Evidence extraction (Product OCR and Product Grounding). Product OCR (19,962 instances) evaluates fine-grained text recognition and specification reading across single product photos, multi-angle gallery views, and long promotional strips. Product Grounding (six benchmarks, 11,939 instances) assesses spatial localization of target products (Product Detection), brand logos (Logo Detection), certification marks (Qualification Detection), specification tables (Chart Detection), dimension annotations (Dimension Detection), and advertised items in livestream frames (Livestream Detection, 1,992 instances). Product interpretation (Product Knowledge, Product Attributes, and Product Retrieval). Product Knowledge (two benchmarks, 4,598 instances) tests fine-grained entity recognition and domain knowledge across products, brands, and industry standards. Product Attributes (four benchmarks, 26,676 instances) evaluates attribute value extraction, brand attribution, and multi-choice property selection from interleaved images and structured fields. Product Retrieval (three benchmarks, 21,584 instances) benchmarks cross-item matching at three granularity levels: judging visual similarity between cropped regions (Regionlevel), determining whether two multimodal listings represent the same product (Product-level), and verifying exact variant equivalence from SKU specifications (SKU-level). Decision making (Product Moderation and E-commerce Reasoning). Product Moderation (three benchmarks, 6,443 instances) evaluates rule-grounded compliance decisions, including detecting prohibited goods, enforcing category sales restrictions, and identifying imagetitle mismatches. E-commerce Reasoning (four benchmarks, 3,500 instances) comprises single-image analytical tasks covering chart reasoning, taxonomy classification, constrained product counting, and spatial relation reasoning, where reference answers are programmatically derived from the underlying product tables and query constraints. 9 Public benchmark coverage. The E-commerce (Open) scenario incorporates 112,415 instances from five public benchmarks: ShoppingMMLU and ChineseEcomQA for e-commerce concepts and operations [4, 32], RAIR for rule-aware search relevance [48], and EcomMMMU and IndustryBench-MIPU for multimodal product understanding and multi-image industrial attribute extraction [41, 63].

sections.title: 4.1 Experimental Setup
sections.content: We evaluate all five WeMM-Ecom models in both thinking and non-thinking modes, using single shared checkpoint per model scale across both operating modes and across both evaluation suites. Our primary comparison pairs each WeMM-Ecom model with the corresponding post-trained Qwen3.5 baseline of the same parameter scale and mode across all 28 e-commerce benchmarks and 64 general-purpose benchmarks. Evaluation protocol. We report the unweighted mean of primary metrics across the 28 e-commerce benchmarks and, separately, across the 64 general benchmarks on 0100 scale (where RefCOCO, RefCOCO+, and RefCOCOg are averaged into single RefCOCO score and the English and Chinese splits of MMBench count as separate benchmarks). Tasks requiring open-ended semantic adjudication use Qwen3-30B-A3BInstruct-2507 [95] as an independent judge, distinct from the Qwen3.5-122B-A10B verifier used during RL training. In flagship comparisons, each external baseline is reported under its best-performing evaluated operating mode, i.e., whichever of thinking and non-thinking mode scores higher for that model. Detailed scoring protocols and decoding settings are provided in Appendix B.

sections.title: 4.2 E-Commerce Results
sections.content: Flagship comparison. Table 3 compares WeMM-Ecom-35B-A3B against leading open-source flagships, including Qwen3.8-Flash-Next [66], HY4 [80], MiMo-V2.6-Flash-RL [65], DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 [12], and GLM-5.3-Flash [103]. Despite having 522 fewer total parameters, WeMM-Ecom-35B-A3B achieves the highest overall average of 74.4 in non-thinking mode, outperforming the strongest baseline, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next (73.2), by about 1.2 points. Substantial gains in Product Retrieval and Product Grounding drive this overall lead  (Table 3)  , which remains consistent under alternative scenario weighting schemes. Dense models. sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: We presented WeMM-Ecom, family of five multimodal large language models ranging from dense 0.8B model to 35B-A3B mixture-of-experts model, together with 28-benchmark e-commerce evaluation suite that spans eight business scenarios and 207,117 instances. Each model is trained with two stages of continued pre-training that raise the e-commerce share from 45.8% to 61.1%, and then post-trained with hybrid-thinking on-policy distillation, single parameter-space merge with the post-trained Qwen3.5 backbone, and GRPO, yielding one checkpoint that serves both thinking and non-thinking modes. Across all ten sizemode comparisons, WeMM-Ecom improves on its Qwen3.5 baseline matched to size in e-commerce while matching or surpassing it on average across the 64 general benchmarks. We also show that WeMM-Ecom-35B-A3B attains the highest e-commerce average among evaluated open-source flagships with 522 fewer total parameters, and WeMM-Ecom-9B surpasses the 3 larger Qwen3.8-27B. This indicates that domain specialization does not necessarily come at the expense of general capabilities, and scale does not gate the specialization benefit. We release all model weights together with our data curation, training recipe, and benchmark construction so that this recipe can be examined and extended in future endeavors regarding domain-specialized models. In production, WeMM-Ecom already serves hundreds of workflows in WeChat E-Commerce, handling billion-scale requests per day across catalog management, multimodal product search, and livestream commerce. Future work will extend WeMM-Ecom to interactive shopping agents and study hardware-aware quantization for real-time edge deployment.

sections.content: A.1 Post-Training Hyperparameters and Prompt Curation Distillation and RL sampling. During OPD, we sample two responses per prompt at temperature 1.0 and top-p 1.0, with maximum generation length of 24,576 tokens within 32,768-token sequence limit. The distillation loss weight is set to 1.0 without an additional reference-policy penalty; compact students (0.8B, 2B, and 4B) initialize from their CPT checkpoints with zero weight decay. During RL, we sample = 16 responses per prompt within 65,536-token context limit using weight decay 0.01, temperature 1.0, and top-p 0.9 by default (supplemented with top-k 20 and repetition penalty 1.05 on instruction-following tasks). All RL runs initialize both the actor and frozen reference policy from the equally weighted (α = 0.5) post-OPD merged checkpoint. Post-training prompt screening. To construct the OPD prompt pool, both the teacher and student models generate eight candidate responses per prompt; we retain prompts where the teacher achieves strictly higher mean quality score than the student. For the RL pool, the corresponding post-OPD merged model generates eight thinking-mode rollouts per candidate prompt. We retain prompts with positive reward variance and mean task reward of at most 0.95, and additionally require strictly positive mean reward on mathematical and logical reasoning tasks. Mode assignment. Operating modes are assigned deterministically by hashing each prompt identifier so that all rollouts for given prompt share the same mode. Thinking mode accounts for 400,229 prompts (80.05%) in the 499,998-prompt OPD pool and 24,823 prompts (80.14%) in the 30,976-prompt RL pool. sections.content: Each instance may contain several images, targets, or products. Benchmark construction and answer adjudication. Table 7 summarizes the 28 e-commerce benchmarks. Product OCR averages accuracies equally across single-image (4,970 instances), multi-image (6,494), and long-image (8,498) subsets. Chart Reasoning averages four 500-question subsets covering SKU charts, price tables, attribute tables, and constraint tables; questions are synthesized under category-specific templates with programmatically computed reference answers and cross-checked by frontier LLMs for reasoning consistency. During evaluation, rule-based matchers first check typed answers and taxonomy aliases before invoking the LLM judge for semantic equivalence. Entity Recognition credits full or partial identifications, Brand tasks allow semantic alias matching, and Image-Title Mismatch requires exact set agreement. Grounding evaluation protocol. All six grounding benchmarks use an IoU threshold of 0.5 with coordinates normalized to [0, 1000]. Chart Detection and Qualification Detection report macro-averaged class F1, whereas the remaining sets report box F1 (with Product Detection using greedy one-to-one matching). In Chart Detection, prompts request JSON objects with bbox_2d and category; to ensure schema compatibility across model families, the evaluation parser also accepts class labels output under the label key when category is absent. In Region-level Retrieval, Spearman rank correlation ρ is Retrieval and public benchmark protocols. linearly rescaled to 50(ρ + 1); for Region-level and Product-level Retrieval, non-thinking mode scores token probabilities whereas thinking mode parses generated labels. Among the public benchmarks, EcomMMMU [41] is evaluated on its labeled general test set (GTS) using the main product image and reported as the unweighted mean across its eight subtasks, while IndustryBench-MIPU [63] uses multi-image product inputs and reports attribute-extraction micro F1.
